label: Operation (surgery)

what_happens.title: What happens on operation day
goals: An operation is how doctors fix or check something inside the body
A special medical sleep means the body does not feel the operation
Waking up comes with a grown-up close by
what_happens.parentSkill: Explain in one sentence what the operation will fix, using the real body part name.

who_is_there.title: Who looks after me
goals: Nurses, the surgeon and the sleep doctor each have a job
People wear masks and caps to keep germs away
who_is_there.parentSkill: Name the three main helpers (nurse, surgeon, sleep doctor) and practise saying hello to each.

what_i_do.title: What I do on operation day
goals: Follow the no-food rule the doctors give
Breathe slowly with the mask, hold a toy
Rest and drink slowly after waking up
what_i_do.parentSkill: Practise breathing through a pretend mask (a cup) and blowing out slowly.

if_scared.title: If it feels scary
goals: It is normal to feel scared before an operation
Waking up may feel sore, sleepy or wobbly, and that passes
Calm tools: slow breaths, a toy, a hand to hold, asking questions
if_scared.parentSkill: Name the feeling and give one true fact: 'You feel scared. The doctors watch over you the whole time.'

rehearsal.title: Let's practise operation day
goals: Play hospital with a toy: gown, name band, mask, wake up
Practise slow breaths with a cup as a mask
End with waking up and a hug
rehearsal.parentSkill: Let your child be the sleep doctor for a toy, then switch roles.

steps: No food for a while before, as the doctors say
Arrive at the hospital and put on a hospital gown and a name band
Meet the nurse, the surgeon and the sleep doctor
Breathe through a mask or get sleep medicine through a little tube
Go into a special deep sleep while the doctors work
Wake up in a recovery room with a grown-up close by
Rest, have a drink and go home or to a hospital room
sensory: a hospital gown that ties at the back
a plastic name band on the wrist
a mask that smells like plastic or a fruity scent
a sleepy, floaty feeling after waking up
a sore spot or a bandage where the doctors worked
a dry mouth and a cold drink
honestyNotes: The child will be in a special medical sleep (anaesthesia) and will not feel the operation while it happens, but may feel sore, sleepy, thirsty or wobbly afterwards. Never call it 'going to sleep' like bedtime and never compare it to a pet being 'put to sleep'. Never promise exactly how long it lasts or that nothing will feel sore. Let the parent fill in what the operation is for.

fallbackAnswer: During the operation you are in a special sleep, so your body does not feel it.
After, the spot may feel sore, and nurses have medicine to help.
Yes. When the doctors finish, the medicine wears off and you wake up.
The sleep doctor watches over you the whole time.

questionButtons.text: Why do I need an operation?
fallbackAnswer: [[GROWNUP]] and the doctors will tell you what they are fixing.
An operation helps your body work better or feel better.
[[GROWNUP]] stays with you before the special sleep, and is there again after you wake up.
Nurses look after you in between.
The mask gives the sleep medicine as air you breathe.
It may smell like plastic or fruit, and you breathe slowly.
An empty tummy keeps you safe during the special sleep.
After, you can have a drink and then food again.
Nurses, the surgeon and the sleep doctor. They all wear name badges.
They wear masks and caps to keep germs away.
You wake up in a quiet room, maybe feeling sleepy or sore.
You rest, have a drink, and then go home or to your room.
Yes, many hospitals let a toy come along, even into the room.
Your toy can be brave with you.

questionButtons.text: What if I wake up during it?
fallbackAnswer: The sleep doctor checks your sleep every second, and that is their whole job.
If you ever need more medicine, they give it.
Some operations leave a small mark that fades over time.
The doctors can tell you what yours will look like.

techniques.label: A comfort toy
techniques.how: Let a favourite toy come to the hospital and into the operating room if allowed.

techniques.label: Mask practice
techniques.how: Breathe slowly through a cup or toy mask at home.

techniques.label: Smell the flower, blow the candle
techniques.how: Breathe in through the nose and out slowly like blowing a candle.

techniques.label: Holding a hand
techniques.how: Hold your child's hand until the special sleep starts.

techniques.label: Asking for a child life specialist
techniques.how: Ask the hospital for a child life specialist who explains each step.

techniques.label: Pain faces scale
techniques.how: Practise pointing to a face from happy to very sore so nurses know how to help.

techniques.label: Hospital tour or video
techniques.how: Watch the hospital's video or take a tour before the day.

techniques.label: Cosy recovery plan
techniques.how: Plan films, books and a treat for the days after.

techniques.label: A question list
techniques.how: Write the child's questions down and ask the doctors together.

pain: During the operation your body is in a special sleep. After, nurses can help if it is sore.
Tell me where it feels sore, so we can help.
body: The doctors are fixing your body so it works better.
The sore spot will get better day by day.
sensory: The mask may smell funny. Breathe slowly.
Beeps are just messages for the nurses.
strangers: The masks keep germs away. They are smiling underneath.
You can ask anyone, what is your job?
separation: I stay with you until you are asleep, and I am there when you wake up.
unknown: First the gown, then the mask, then a special sleep, then waking up.
We will ask the doctors every question.
safety: The sleep doctor watches over you the whole time.
When they finish, you wake up.
social: Lots of kids have operations and get better.
Your friends can send you pictures.
love: I love you, and I'm proud of you.
We will have cosy days together after.

sentences.text: Soon [[CHILD]] will have an operation.
An operation is a way doctors fix or check something inside the body.
First [[CHILD]] and [[GROWNUP]] go to the hospital.
Then [[CHILD]] puts on a hospital gown and a name band.
Before bed, here is a story about a little bear called Bo.
Bo had a sore paw that needed fixing.
Mama Bear said, the forest doctors will do an operation to fix your paw.
First they went to the big tree hospital.
Then Bo put on a soft gown with little stars.
Next the owl doctor said, I am the sleep doctor.
This special medicine helps your body go into a deep sleep, so the doctors can work.
It is a different sleep from bedtime, and I watch over you the whole time.
Bo held Mama's paw, and breathed slowly.
Then the story says, Bo woke up later, and Mama was right there.
Tomorrow evening, the story goes on.
Next a sleep doctor gives a special medicine through a mask or a tiny tube.
It makes the body go into a deep, special sleep, different from bedtime sleep.
While the body sleeps, the doctors do their work carefully.
After that, [[CHILD]] wakes up in a quiet room, and a grown-up is close by.
[[CHILD]] can ask, what will you fix, and the doctors will explain.

Anaesthesia is the medical name for the special sleep, and the doctor who gives it is an anaesthetist.
This doctor watches breathing, heart rate and oxygen on a screen the whole time.
Under anaesthesia the brain does not notice the operation and does not remember it.
Waking up can feel groggy, and that passes in a few hours.
[[CHILD]] can ask the anaesthetist to explain each machine before the operation.
An operating room is very clean, cool and bright, with big lights so the surgeon can see clearly.
Everyone has a job: the surgeon operates, the anaesthetist manages the sleep, and nurses pass tools and keep track of everything.
They check the name band and the plan many times, because being careful is part of the job.
In many hospitals [[GROWNUP]] can stay until [[CHILD]] is asleep.
[[CHILD]] can ask to meet the team before the operation.
The no-food rule matters: an empty stomach keeps the airway safe during anaesthesia.
Some kids choose to breathe the mask gas, and some get the medicine through a small tube called an IV.
Waking up, it is normal to feel confused, cold, thirsty or a bit sick for a while.
Pain medicine helps with soreness afterwards, and nurses check often.
[[CHILD]] can rate the pain from one to ten so the nurses know how to help.
It is normal to worry about waking up during the operation; the anaesthetist checks the sleep every second, which is exactly their job.
Soreness afterwards is expected and treated, not something to be brave about in silence.
Some kids feel emotional or teary when they wake up, which is the medicine wearing off.
[[CHILD]] can write down three questions to ask the doctors.
[[CHILD]] can ask for a child life specialist, a helper whose job is explaining hospital things.
Knowing the plan step by step makes the day feel more under control.
[[CHILD]] can make a list: what to pack, what to ask, and what to do after, like a film or a game.
Many hospitals offer a tour or a video of the operating room for kids.
Planning a reward for the recovery days gives something to look forward to.
[[CHILD]] can choose the comfort item that goes into the operating room.
